certainty_reasoning: Proposed 'consensus', not 'documented-sexual'. The primary evidence read for this file - Wilde's letters to Ross 1888-1900 and Ross's December 1900 letters - documents a lifelong bond of the first intimacy (affectionate registers rising to 'Yours, with much love' by 1889, shared secrets, daily attendance in the final illness, the deathbed, the executorship) but contains no first-person statement of sexual relations. The sexual reading, standard across major biographers, rests on later Ross statements reported in secondary literature not yet read in the source for this project (Ellmann/McKenna verification is a standing next step). Dating tension to preserve: the biographical tradition makes Ross Wilde's first male lover from c. 1886, the year they met, but Ross himself, to Adela Schuster (14 Dec. 1900), wrote that he 'only became intimate with him when he was writing Lady Windermere' - i.e. c. 1891 - with 'long intervals when I never saw him' and no regular correspondence 'until after the downfall'. Start is the documented 1886 meeting; the onset of any sexual phase is deliberately not sharpened.
date_label: Met 1886 (Ross: 'I only met him in '86'); Ross dated the intimacy to the Lady Windermere period, c. 1891; regular correspondence only after the downfall; to Wilde's death, 30 Nov. 1900, with Ross at the bedside; literary executor thereafter.
summary: Ross met Wilde in 1886 and remained, in the editors' words, 'his most faithful friend until Wilde's death when he became the literary executor to the estate'. The surviving correspondence opens in October 1888 ('My dear Bobbie … I shall miss you in town') and by 1889 runs to 'Yours, with much love'; Ross himself dated their intimacy to the period when Wilde was writing Lady Windermere (c. 1891). After 1895 Ross became the relationship's practical center - regular correspondent, supervisor of the De Profundis typescript at his Hornton Street lodgings, daily attendant of the final illness who fetched the priest for Wilde's deathbed reception into the Catholic Church - and he was holding Wilde's hand at the death on 30 November 1900. He buried Wilde at Bagneux in a concession hired in his own name, moved the remains to Père Lachaise in 1909, and administered the literary estate.

sources.quote: No other friend have I now in this beautiful world. I want no other. … My poem should have run, 'When I came out of prison you met me with garments, with spices, with wise counsel. You met me with love.' Not others did it, but you.
sources.context: Wilde to Robert Ross, [28 May 1897], Hôtel de la Plage, Berneval-sur-Mer - his first days out of prison, alone for the first time. Editors' n. 2 gives the lines in their verse form and records that they were intended as a second dedication to The Ballad of Reading Gaol and removed at proof stage.
sources.supports: Wilde naming what Ross was to him, in his own words: the one friend left to him, and the one who met him at his release with love rather than counsel - the most explicit first-hand characterization of the bond in the correspondence read

sources.quote: Robert Baldwin Ross (1869–1918) was a Canadian. … He first met Wilde in 1886 and remained his most faithful friend until Wilde's death when he became the literary executor to the estate.
sources.context: Holland & Hart-Davis, biographical footnote on Ross, hung on Wilde's first surviving letter to him (c. 13 October 1888); the note asserts friendship and executorship only, no sexual claim
sources.supports: Frame of the bond: met 1886; 'most faithful friend' to Wilde's death; literary executor

sources.quote: But I only met him in '86 and only became intimate with him when he was writing Lady Windermere, but there were long intervals when I never saw him, and he never corresponded with me regularly until after the downfall.
sources.context: Ross to Adela Schuster, 14 December 1900, printed in the Epilogue; 'Lady Windermere' italicized in the original; Ross declining the suggestion that he become Wilde's Boswell
sources.supports: Ross's own timeline: met Wilde 1886, intimacy only from the Lady Windermere period (c. 1891) - complicates the common claim that the liaison began in 1886

sources.quote: I went to the bedside and held his hand, his pulse began to flutter. He heaved a deep sigh, the only natural one I had heard since I arrived, the limbs seemed to stretch involuntarily, the breathing came fainter; he passed at 10 minutes to 2 p.m. exactly.
sources.context: Ross to More Adey, 14 December 1900, narrating Wilde's death at the Hôtel d'Alsace, Paris, on 30 November 1900; Ross and Reggie Turner were the two friends present
sources.supports: Ross at the bedside holding Wilde's hand at the moment of death - the terminal point of the lifelong bond

sources.quote: Little did Eliza Ross or Constance Wilde suspect, when they finalized this arrangement, that some time the previous year, the thirty-two-year-old Oscar and the seventeen-year-old Robbie had become lovers.
sources.context: Fryer introducing Ross's 1887 residence as the Wildes' lodger at 16 Tite Street, Chelsea. The biographer's own assertion, not a participant's words. Ages stated exactly as Fryer states them (README register rule).
sources.supports: Ross's dedicated biographer dates the start of a sexual relationship to 1886 - the traditional dating, against which Ross's own 1900 letter to Adela Schuster stands.

sources.quote: Whatever the precise circumstances of the contact being forged, it would appear that young Robbie seduced Oscar some time in 1886, and that this was Oscar's first experience of a homosexual act.   Oscar told his friend, the journalist and wit Reggie Turner, that this was the case.   Robbie himself later confirmed it to one of Wilde's earliest biographers, Arthur Ransome.
sources.context: Same page, after Fryer dismisses Frank Harris's public-lavatory story of the first meeting. Fryer gives no note for these sentences; neither Wilde's remark to Turner nor Ross's confirmation to Ransome is quoted or sourced on the page.
sources.supports: A reported chain of PARTICIPANT testimony for the 1886 dating - Wilde told Turner, Ross told Ransome - which is the nearest thing Fryer offers to first-person evidence. It remains Fryer's report of an unsourced oral confirmation, not the participant's surviving words: a lead toward self-reported evidence rather than an instance of it.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 32, printed folio 18 confirmed on the rendered page, read as page image 2026-08-03. Contiguous sentences; the preceding block on the same page is quoted separately, with no elision joining them.

sources.quote: It should not be assumed, however, that Oscar and Robbie conducted a passionate, clandestine affair on the premises.   On the contrary, it is unlikely that they did, and not only for reasons of propriety.   Despite the initial seduction, and the huge bond of affection between them, neither was physically each other's 'type'.
sources.context: Fryer on the months of 1887 when Ross lodged at Tite Street. He continues that Ross 'was far more interested sexually in youths of his own age than in the rather portly, flabby, albeit fascinating Oscar Wilde.'
sources.supports: Fryer separates a single initiating episode in 1886 from a sustained affair, and denies the latter for 1887 - supplying the middle term under which the 1886 tradition and Ross's own 'only became intimate... Lady Windermere' (1900) can both be true. Fryer never cites the Schuster letter, so the reconciliation is available from him but not stated by him.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 35, printed folio 21 confirmed on the rendered page, read as page image 2026-08-03.

sources.quote: In fact, Robbie was already, at the age of nineteen, much more than a disciple and sometime lover for Oscar.   The two could talk frankly, despite the difference in their ages, and bounce ideas off each other.
sources.context: Fryer at the turn of 1888-89, Ross's first year at King's College, Cambridge. Age stated exactly as Fryer states it.
sources.supports: Fryer's summary formula for the bond - 'disciple and sometime lover'. 'Sometime' is his word, and his second signal that he does not read the relationship as a continuous affair.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 47, printed folio 33 confirmed on the rendered page, read as page image 2026-08-03.

sources.quote: Robbie seems to have felt no jealousy towards John Gray.   Indeed, he was remarkably generous and understanding when it came to Oscar's other lovers.   Of course, he himself was enjoying various encounters with youths, though none at this stage held any claim to his affections, let alone to the sort of love he felt for Oscar.
sources.context: c. 1889-90, immediately before the family council that sent Ross to Edinburgh away from 'myriad temptations, including Oscar Wilde'. Fryer's own characterisation of Ross's feeling; no participant statement is quoted.
sources.supports: The asymmetry Fryer builds the life on: Ross in love with Wilde and unpossessive about Gray and Wilde's other lovers, while sexually occupied elsewhere. Bears on the ross--wilde bond and on why no jealousy edge to gray or douglas is warranted.
